cards.explanation: The answer is False. Verse 1 puts Ahaz next to David and then says, “And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD.” Chronicles doesn't ease into it, friends. The first verse already tells you which way this reign is headed.

The answer is cast images of the Baals. Verse 2 says Ahaz walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and “…even made cast images of the Baals.” Notice the word “even,” friends. It comes right before the images.

The answer is the king of Aram. Verse 5 says the LORD delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Aram, who attacked him and took many captives. Chronicles says this happened after what the last few verses described. And Aram is only the first hit, bakers. Another one comes in the same verse.
The answer is Damascus. Verse 5 says the king of Aram “…took many captives to Damascus.” Keep that name handy, friends, because Damascus comes back later in this chapter.

The answer is True, and the verse says it plainly. “For in one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah.” Then it gives the reason: “This happened because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.” A hundred and twenty thousand in a single day. That's a heavy verse, friends.

The answer is Samaria. Verse 8 says the Israelites took the captives and a great deal of plunder and brought it to Samaria. That's also where the army is heading when a prophet walks out to meet it in the next verse, bakers.

The answer is because of His wrath against Judah. That's what Oded says. “Look,” he tells the army, “because of His wrath against Judah, the LORD, the God of your fathers, has delivered them into your hand.” He starts there, friends, and notice he doesn't pat the army on the back. The very next line begins with “But.”

The answer is False. Oded says the army plans to enslave the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem, and then he asks, “…are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?” He's not giving them a pass, friends. He's telling a whole army to look at itself.

The answer is captives. Oded says, “…return the captives you took from your kinsmen, for the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you.” He isn't asking them to think it over, bakers. He's telling them to hand the people back.

The answer is that it would add to Israel's guilt before the LORD. The Ephraimite leaders say, “You must not bring the captives here, for you are proposing to bring guilt upon us from the LORD and to add to our sins and our guilt.” These leaders know Israel's guilt is already big, friends, and they don't want to pile more on top.

The answer is Jericho. Verse 15 says they brought the captives “…to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers.” Then the men returned to Samaria. Along the way, friends, they put all the feeble on donkeys.

The answer is the king of Assyria. Verse 16 says, “At that time King Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria.” Keep an eye on this one, friends. Verse 20 says Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to Ahaz but “…afflicted him rather than strengthening him.”

The answer is that Ahaz had been most unfaithful to the LORD. Verse 19 says the LORD humbled Judah because Ahaz “…had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD.” Chronicles gives the cause right there, bakers. It doesn't leave us guessing.
The answer is True. Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came to Ahaz but “…afflicted him rather than strengthening him.” Ahaz sent for help and got hurt instead, friends. Not what he had in mind.

The answer is False. The text says, “In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.” Hard times can make a person turn back, friends, but that's not what this verse says happened. Ahaz didn't turn back to the LORD.

The answer is that he thinks they helped Aram and might help him. That's his own reasoning. Ahaz says, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” Then the text adds, “But these gods were the downfall of Ahaz and of all Israel.” His plan didn't hold up, friends.

The answer is shuts. Verse 24 says Ahaz cut the articles of the house of God into pieces and “…shut the doors of the house of the LORD…” The place was closed up, friends. I think this is the saddest verse in the whole chapter.

The answer is on every street corner in Jerusalem. Verse 24 says he “…set up altars of his own on every street corner in Jerusalem.” Every single street corner, bakers. He didn't pick one spot, he spread them across the city.

The answer is False. Verse 27 says Ahaz was buried in the city of Jerusalem, “…but he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel.” That's a quiet end to a loud reign, friends. And the verse ends with his son Hezekiah taking his place.
